approachQuestion.prompt:
Exactly k Visitor Types

Given an integer array `visits` and positive k, count non-empty contiguous segments containing exactly k different identifiers. Segments are distinguished by indices.

Limits and assumptions:
• 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ k ≤ 200000; -10^9 ≤ visits[i] ≤ 10^9.
• The answer fits in signed 64-bit integers. Keep visits unchanged.

Examples:
1. visits = [1,2,1,3], k = 2 → 4: [0,1], [0,2], [1,2], [2,3].
2. visits = [7,7], k = 1 → 3.

Choose one approach.
constraints: The answer fits in signed 64-bit integers. Keep visits unchanged.

options.text: Define F(t) as the number of segments with at most t distinct identifiers, using a frequency window and adding its valid suffix count at each end. Return F(k) - F(k-1), with F(0)=0.
options.feedback: The subtraction removes exactly the segments with fewer than k types; each F counts all valid starts, rather than just endpoints.

options.text: For every start, build a fresh frequency table while extending the end, count segments with exactly k types, and stop after more than k types appear.
options.feedback: All legal segments are counted, but overlapping scans and rebuilt counts repeat work that two boundary sweeps can share.

options.text: Return F(k), counting every segment with at most k types.
options.feedback: For [1,2], k=2 this counts three segments although only the pair has exactly two types.

options.text: Shrink until at most k types remain, then add one whenever exactly k remain.
options.feedback: For [7,7], k=1 there are three qualifying segments but this adds only twice.

feedback.reason: Segments with exactly k types are those counted by F(k) but not F(k-1).
details: Run F(k) and F(k-1) sequentially. For F(t), keep counts of active identifiers, deleting zero counts, and shrink until at most t types remain. Add right-left+1. For t=0 return zero. Subtract the two totals; release the first table before the second run.

Segments with exactly k types are those counted by F(k) but not F(k-1). Each F adds every valid suffix count, not one per endpoint. Release the first frequency table before the second sweep; the two passes add time rather than multiply it.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only “Subtract two inclusive counts” as specified in the method reveal. Choose the tightest worst-case running-time and auxiliary-space pair under the stated expected hashing model.
constraints: Hash table lookup, insert, and delete have expected constant cost with amortized resizing; include allocated table capacity. Zero-count keys are deleted.
n is visits.length. Arithmetic and random access are unit cost, with 64-bit counters. Input and scalar output are excluded.
The two passes are sequential and iterative, with no copied segments and a constant call stack.

options.text: Expected O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Two sequential at-most sweeps have expected linear total work.
details: Each F advances both boundaries at most n times and performs expected constant-time table operations per move. Two sequential passes still use expected O(n) time and at most n stored keys. The sets counted by F(k-1) are exactly the non-exact segments in F(k).
“O(n²) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Each at-most pass advances both boundaries across n entries, and two sequential passes add their costs rather than multiplying them.
“O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Non-adversarial hash operations have expected constant cost here; neither pass sorts keys or uses a logarithmic search structure.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: F(k) can retain n distinct identifiers. Releasing one table before the next does not make a single growing table constant-sized.
